findings.where: paper/main.tex, abstract (l. 92–94) and Contribution 2 (l. 183–189); the reported interval is defined at main.tex l. 518–521; the only bound on the curvature error is Thm. thm:curv, l. 381–394
findings.claim: The headline wedge — "the resulting estimator of $S$ converges at $\widetilde{O}(N^{-1/2})$, against $N^{-1/8}$ for iterate-based batch means under dependence" — compares an estimator of $S$ with estimators of the whole sandwich $\Sigma=H^{-1}SH^{-1}$, and the paper never states a rate for the object it actually reports.
findings.why:
Zhu et al., Roy–Balasubramanian and Samsonov et al. estimate $\Sigma$ (that is the point of being Hessian-free); the paper's $\widetilde O(N^{-1/2})$ is for $S$ alone. The quantity that sets the interval half-width is $u_j^{	op}\Sft u_j$ with $u_j=\Hb^{-1}e_j$, and the only bound available for $\Hb^{-1}$ is thm:curv: "for every $
u_H<\min\{\varrho,1/2\}$, $\opnorm{\Hb_t^{-1}-H^{-1}}=O(t^{-
u_H})$" with $\varrho\in(0,1/2)$. So the reported variance estimate has relative error $O_p(N^{-
u_H})$, $
u_H<\varrho<1/2$ — strictly slower than $N^{-1/2}$, equal to $N^{-0.4}$ at the paper's own default $\varrho=0.4$ (src/bgsn/estimators.py: ci_pow=0.4), and *worse* than the $N^{-1/8}$ it claims to beat for any $\varrho\le1/8$. The appendix proof of thm:lrv confirms only consistency here ("$\Hb^{-1}	o_pH^{-1}$ ... and Slutsky gives the studentised limit", sec_appendix.tex l. 273–275) — no rate. A referee will read the abstract as a claim about asymptotic-covariance estimation and find that the paper's own theorems do not support it.
findings.fix: Either (a) prove a rate for the sandwich $\opnorm{\Hb^{-1}\Sft\Hb^{-1}-\Sigma}=O_p(N^{-\nu_H}+\sqrt{\log N/N})$ and quote *that* number when comparing with iterate-based estimators (sharpening thm:curv, e.g. letting $\varrho\uparrow1/2$ or switching off the ridge asymptotically, so the composite is $\widetilde O(N^{-1/2})$), or (b) rewrite the abstract/Contribution 2 to say explicitly that the $\widetilde O(N^{-1/2})$ is for the score long-run covariance $S$, that the competing $N^{-1/8}$ rates are for the full sandwich, and state the composite rate the intervals actually inherit.

findings.where: paper/sec_related.tex l. 18–20 ("none of it estimates an asymptotic variance"); refs.bib (116 entries, no Godichon-Baggioni 2019)
findings.claim: The sentence "All of this work assumes independent observations, and none of it estimates an asymptotic variance: these papers prove central limit theorems but stop there" is false, and the counterexample is an uncited paper by the author of the base method.
findings.why: Godichon-Baggioni, "Online estimation of the asymptotic variance for averaged stochastic gradient algorithms", JSPI 2019 (arXiv:1702.00931), gives exactly what the sentence says nobody gives: "a new recursive algorithm for estimating this last one [the asymptotic variance], and we establish its almost sure rate of convergence as well as its rate of convergence in quadratic mean", with logistic regression as an application. It is absent from refs.bib (grep for godichon returns only bercu2020efficient, boyer2023asymptotic, cenac2025efficient, godichonbaggioni2023learning/2023nonasymptotic/2024online/2025adaptive/2026complexity). The most likely referee for this paper is that author. It also removes the novelty of the framing "turning the central limit theorem into usable intervals" (sec_related.tex l. 23–24) as an unmet need in this line — the unmet need is specifically the *long-run* variance under dependence. Also missing: Jiang, Roy, Balasubramanian, Davis, Drusvyatskiy & Na, "Online Covariance Estimation in Nonsmooth Stochastic Approximation" (arXiv:2502.05305), another batch-means-at-$n^{-1/8}$ entry in the same family.
findings.fix: Cite Godichon-Baggioni (2019) in the intro's "What we do not claim" list and in sec_related, and replace the absolute sentence with the accurate one: recursive/online estimation of the *instantaneous* sandwich for averaged first-order and Newton-type streaming methods exists under i.i.d. data (Godichon-Baggioni 2019; Chen et al. 2020; Kuang et al.; Wang et al.), and what is missing there is the long-run object under dependence. Add arXiv:2502.05305 to the batch-means list.

findings.where: paper/main.tex Contribution 3, l. 194–202 ("The mechanism is not ours; the bias order under mixing is"); proof in paper/sec_appendix.tex l. 218–237
findings.claim: The one thing Contribution 3 claims as new — the $O(\rho^b)$ bias order of the flat-top/lugsail correction under geometric mixing — is the standard tail-sum property of flat-top windows, and the paper never confronts the closest prior statement of it.
findings.why: The appendix proof is four lines of window algebra plus Davydov: the weights are "exactly $1$ for $|k|\le b$ and $(2b-|k|)/b$ ... so $\dots=S-\sum_{|k|\ge2b}\Gamma_k-\sum_{b<|k|<2b}(1-\frac{2b-|k|}{b})\Gamma_k=S+O(\rho^{b})$". Nothing about the algorithm, the iterate, or block gradients enters; it is the generic fact that a flat-top window's bias is bounded by the autocovariance tail, hence exponentially small when $\Gamma_k$ decays geometrically. That is precisely the selling point of the flat-top literature the paper cites for the "mechanism" only: Politis (2011) is titled/abstracted as "higher-order accurate ... when higher-order accuracy is possible", and the Politis–Romano flat-top papers state near-$\sqrt N$ consistency when the autocovariance is compactly supported or decays fast. Singh et al.'s open problem is an *exact bias expression* under i.i.d. SGD dynamics, not the tail-bias order for a mixing sequence, so "it is what the SGD literature using this correction leaves open" mis-locates the gap.
findings.fix: Demote Contribution 3: credit the tail-sum bias order to the flat-top literature explicitly ("for a stationary sequence with geometrically decaying autocovariances this is the classical flat-top tail bound; see Politis & Romano 1995, Politis 2011"), and claim instead the two things that are genuinely yours: that block *gradients* put you in that regime with $b\asymp\log N$ (data mixing, not iterate mixing), and the drift control $\tau_{b,N}=(b+d)\log^2N/N$ that shows a moving iterate does not destroy it. Add one sentence in sec_related saying what is new relative to Politis's near-$\sqrt N$ result.

findings.where: paper/main.tex Contribution 2, l. 185–189 ("forces $b\asymp N^{3/4}$ and caps the rate at $N^{-1/8}$"); cf. paper/sec_related.tex l. 32–35 and main.tex rem:whyfast l. 560–564
findings.claim: "Caps the rate at $N^{-1/8}$" for iterate-path batch means is contradicted by the paper's own related-work section and by its own displayed formula in rem:whyfast.
findings.why: sec_related.tex l. 32–35 says "\citet{ni2026online} improve the batch-means rate to $N^{-1/6}$ and establish the minimax rate $\Theta(N^{-(1-a)/2})$ for Hessian-free covariance estimation from the iterate path" — i.e. the block-growth exponent the paper says is "forced" is exactly what Ni & Huo re-tune (their abstract: "Re-tuning the block-growth parameter improves the batch-means rate to $O(n^{-(1-\alpha)/3})$", arXiv:2604.10814). And rem:whyfast's own algebra, "which requires $b\asymp N^{a}$ and yields rates of order $N^{-1/8}$", gives $\sqrt{b/N}=N^{(a-1)/2}$, which is $N^{-1/8}$ only at $a=3/4$ and tends to $N^{-1/4}$ as $a\downarrow1/2$. Zhu et al. is also an i.i.d. result, so citing it for what "dependent sampling forces" is loose. The honest ceiling for the trajectory class is $\Theta(N^{-1/4})$, not $N^{-1/8}$, which halves the advertised exponent gap.
findings.fix: Replace "caps the rate at $N^{-1/8}$" with "the best published rates under dependent sampling are $N^{-1/8}$ (Roy & Balasubramanian; Samsonov et al.), and the minimax ceiling for the whole Hessian-free trajectory class is $\Theta(N^{-(1-a)/2})$, i.e. no better than $N^{-1/4}$". State the comparison against that ceiling, not against one tuning.

findings.where: paper/main.tex rem:whyfast, l. 567–569; contradicted by paper/sec_experiments.tex l. 19–27 ("Methods compared")
findings.claim: The exclusivity claim "it is available only to an algorithm that forms block gradients and keeps a curvature estimate" is contradicted by the paper's own experiments, and it mislocates the novelty wedge.
findings.why: sec_experiments.tex l. 22–27 runs "averaged SGD and streaming AdaGrad with tuned step sizes, each with the i.i.d. plug-in, with our long-run variance, or with random scaling" and notes "First-order baselines are given the *true* Hessian" — i.e. the block-gradient $S$-estimator is demonstrably method-agnostic: any method that sees per-observation gradients (all of them do) can average them over blocks of length $\log N$. The only thing the quasi-Newton structure supplies is $\Hb^{-1}$ for free. So the wedge is "plug-in/gradient-based (needs $H$) versus Hessian-free (iterate-path)" — a distinction that already exists in the i.i.d. literature the paper cites (chen2020statistical's plug-in) — not "quasi-Newton versus first-order". A referee will say the paper's central rate claim is really a claim about the plug-in family, and will ask why an averaged-SGD-plus-recursive-Hessian baseline is not the headline comparator.
findings.fix: Reword to "available to any algorithm that observes the individual gradients and can supply a curvature estimate; the quasi-Newton recursion is what makes the curvature estimate free", and add one sentence in Contribution 2 and sec_related placing the construction in the plug-in family (Chen et al. 2020; Godichon-Baggioni 2019) with HAC/flat-top weights replacing $\widehat\Gamma_0$.

findings.where: paper/main.tex Contribution 2 l. 189–191 and rem:whyfast l. 569–571; paper/sec_limits.tex l. 49–53
findings.claim: The stated reason the Ni & Huo minimax bound does not apply — "a quasi-Newton method is not in that class, because it already maintains curvature" — is inaccurate: their own minimax-optimal estimator builds a Hessian estimate.
findings.why: Ni & Huo's optimal construction is a "trajectory-regression estimator [that] estimates the Hessian by regressing SGD increments on iterates" (arXiv:2604.10814 abstract). "Hessian-free" there means no second-derivative oracle, not "does not form a curvature estimate"; the class is defined by the *information* observed (the iterate path). Maintaining curvature therefore does not put you outside it — observing the individual/block gradients and the $\alpha\Phi\Phi^{\top}$ curvature oracle does. As written, the escape clause is wrong on its face to anyone who has read the cited paper, and it appears three times (contributions, rem:whyfast, sec_limits), so it reads as the paper's considered position rather than a slip. sec_limits.tex l. 50–53 is closer ("because we use more information (block gradients and a maintained curvature estimate)") but still lists curvature-maintenance as the operative difference.
findings.fix: State the escape in information terms only: "their lower bound is over estimators measurable with respect to the iterate path; our estimator uses the per-observation gradients and the curvature oracle $\alpha\Phi\Phi^{\top}$, so it is outside that class — note their own optimal estimator does form a Hessian estimate, by regressing increments on iterates, which is why maintaining curvature is not itself the distinction. We make no optimality claim within our information set."

findings.where: paper/main.tex fig:lrvrate caption, l. 640–648; paper/sec_experiments.tex l. 19–27
findings.claim: The rate wedge is never measured against an actual iterate-based batch-means estimator; the "$b\asymp N^{3/4}$ schedule that iterate-based batch means require" is the paper's own estimator run at a bad block length, which is a straw man.
findings.why: The caption says that schedule "is shown for reference and is much worse here, because it leaves too few blocks" — but Zhu et al. and Samsonov et al. use *overlapping/recursive* windows over the entire trajectory precisely so that long blocks do not leave few effective batches, so "too few blocks" is not the failure mode of the estimator being displaced. The "Methods compared" list contains an offline HAC reference and random scaling but no recursive overlapping-batch-means-of-iterates baseline, so the paper's central quantitative claim (T2) has no empirical head-to-head at all.
findings.fix: Implement the actual comparator — recursive overlapping batch means on the iterate path (Zhu et al. 2023 / Roy & Balasubramanian 2023 recursion) on at least the AR-hom design — and plot its $\opnorm{\widehat\Sigma-\Sigma}$ against the composite $\opnorm{\Hb^{-1}\Sft\Hb^{-1}-\Sigma}$. Retitle the third curve in fig:lrvrate as "our estimator at $b\asymp N^{3/4}$ (block-length sensitivity)", not as what iterate-based batch means require.

findings.where: paper/main.tex fig:lrv caption l. 634–635 ("our block length need not grow with $N$") versus Thm. thm:lrv hypothesis (l. 534: "let $b=b_N\to\infty$ with $b_N=o(N)$"); Contribution 4 l. 203–207
findings.claim: Two small credit/consistency slips in the claim statements: the figure caption asserts a stronger result than the theorem allows, and Contribution 4 credits prior art anonymously.
findings.why: thm:lrv requires $b_N\to\infty$ (the $O(\rho^b)$ bias only vanishes that way), and every rate statement uses $b\asymp\log N$; "need not grow with $N$" is true only for the *point estimate* (thm:as, "for every fixed block length $b\ge1$"). The correct wedge is "grows only logarithmically", and overstating it invites a referee to check the theorem and find the mismatch. Separately, Contribution 4 says "reproduce a previously reported qualitative failure quantitatively" with no citation in the contributions list; the credit to liu2026statistical appears only later in the body (main.tex l. 490–493). Since the contributions list is where boundaries are read, an unattributed "previously reported" reads as evasive.
findings.fix: Change the caption to "which is why our block length need only grow like $\log N$". Attach \citep{liu2026statistical} inside Contribution 4 ("the qualitative failure was reported by ...; we give the exact limit and verify it to three decimals").

findings.where: paper/sec_appendix.tex, Lemma lem:series (l.33-46) and its three applications: proof of thm:as (l.128-133), term (A) (l.162-166), term (C) (l.173-179)
findings.claim: lem:series is stated for "a bounded **deterministic** sequence" (a_t) of weights and centred stationary summands, but in every place where it is invoked to replace the martingale argument the weights are random, data-dependent and correlated with the summand, so the lemma does not apply and the claimed remainder orders are unproved.
findings.why: In term (A) the summand is (H^{-1}-P_{t-1})eps_t and the proof says "lem:series with a_t=t^{-nu_H}", i.e. it substitutes a deterministic bound for a random matrix coefficient — a norm bound on a sum cannot be obtained that way. Worse, under dependence E[(H^{-1}-P_{t-1})eps_t] != 0 (this is exactly what the paper says destroys the martingale property, main.tex l.396: "E[eps_t | F_{t-1}] != 0"), so the summand is not centred and the lemma's hypothesis fails outright. The only bound the paper's own toolkit supplies is Davydov across the one-block gap: |E[(H^{-1}-P_{t-1})eps_t]| <= C rho^0 t^{-nu_H} b^{-1}, whose Cesaro average is O(b^{-1} T^{-nu_H}); since thm:curv only delivers nu_H < min{varrho,1/2} = varrho < 1/2, this is NOT o(T^{-1/2}), so the claim (A)=o(T^{-1/2}) does not follow and thm:rate/thm:clt/prop:blockfree are unsupported. Same defect in thm:as, where a_t = gamma_t||P_{t-1}|| ||grad F(theta_{t-1})|| is F_{t-1}-measurable and correlated with eps_t; the sentence "a localisation argument on the events {sup_{s<=t}||theta_s||<=K} removes the dependence of the weights on the future" is a non-sequitur — localisation controls boundedness, not the a_t–zeta_t correlation, which is precisely the non-martingale problem. In term (C) the summand zeta_t=(Hhat_t-H)delta_{t-1} is neither stationary nor centred, and the displayed output O(T^{-1}(sum_t b^{-1}t^{-1})^{1/2}log^{1/2+eps}T) is not what a lemma with a_t=1 returns (that would give T^{1/2}); variances have been silently substituted for weights. This is the paper's announced "technical substitute for the martingale argument" (main.tex l.409-411), so the gap sits under T1 in its entirety.
findings.fix: Either (i) prove a conditionally-weighted version of lem:series for F_{t-1}-measurable weights under mixing (e.g. via the Poisson-equation/martingale-plus-remainder route the paper explicitly declines at main.tex l.397-400), or (ii) bound term (A) by exploiting the structure the crude bound throws away: P_{t-1}-H^{-1} ~ -H^{-1}(Hbar_{t-1}-H)H^{-1} is an average of n_{t-1} curvature terms of which only O(1) lie within mixing range of block t, giving E[(H^{-1}-P_{t-1})eps_t]=O(1/(tb)) and hence O(log T/(bT)) after averaging. Whichever route, the martingale-free control of random-weight mixing sums must be stated as a lemma and proved, not obtained by plugging deterministic bounds into lem:series.

findings.where: paper/sec_appendix.tex, proof of lem:series, l.51-56 (the cited Bernstein inequality)
findings.claim: The Merlevede–Peligrad–Rio inequality is cited in a form that is false under the lemma's hypotheses: their Theorem 1 requires uniformly **bounded** summands (||X_i||_inf <= M) and its denominator carries M*lambda*(log n)^2, whereas lem:series assumes only E||zeta_1||^{2+nu} < infinity and the paper writes "lambda a_max log T_0".
findings.why: No inequality of the displayed exponential form can hold under a polynomial moment assumption. Take T_0 = 4 and a single heavy-tailed zeta with exactly 2+nu moments: the true tail P(max_{T<=4}||M_T|| >= lambda) decays like lambda^{-(2+nu)}, while the quoted bound decays like exp(-C lambda/(a_max log 4)) — the bound is violated for large lambda. Since the boundedness constant M is what the quoted 'a_max' has silently replaced, the whole dyadic-block + Borel–Cantelli step has no valid input. Both halves of lem:series therefore rest on nothing, including the a_n == 1 maximal half that thm:curv relies on (l.96-99: "Applying lem:series with a_n = 1 ... gives ||sum_{n<=n_t}(Y_n-H)|| = O(n_t^{1/2} log^{1/2+eps} n_t)"), which is the only control of the new term (iii) in the curvature recursion. The conclusions are plausible (an LIL-type rate for geometrically mixing sequences with 2+delta moments is available), but they must be sourced from a result whose hypotheses the paper actually satisfies.
findings.fix: Replace the MPR citation by a maximal inequality / a.s. invariance principle for strongly mixing sequences under finite (2+nu)-moments — e.g. Rio's maximal inequality (Rio 2017, Thm 6.3 / 6.4) or the Oodaira–Yoshihara LIL for alpha-mixing sequences — and re-derive eq:maximal from it; if MPR Thm 1 is kept, add a truncation argument (truncate at M_T = T^{1/(2+nu)}, control the tail by Markov + Borel–Cantelli) and correct the denominator to include (log T_0)^2.

findings.where: paper/main.tex thm:curv (l.373-386) vs paper/sec_appendix.tex proof of thm:as (l.118-119) and proof of thm:rate (l.168-171); ridge definition main.tex l.270-273
findings.claim: The theorem dependency graph is circular as written and the induction is never stated: thm:curv *hypothesises* the rate ||theta_t-theta*|| = O(t^{-1/2}log^c t); thm:as's proof uses thm:curv ("gamma_t^2||P_{t-1}||^2 = O(t^{2varrho-2}) by thm:curv"); thm:rate then derives that very rate by "Bootstrapping from ||delta_t||=o(1) (thm:as) through eq:decomp", whose terms (A),(B) are bounded using thm:curv.
findings.why: A reader cannot verify the argument because the staging is not given: thm:curv as stated is a conditional statement whose hypothesis is supplied only by thm:rate, which uses thm:curv. The fix exists (the ridge bound lambda_min(Hbar_t) >= c n_t^{-varrho} in the proof is derived without any rate, and term (iv) with only ||delta_t||=o(1) still gives ||Hbar_t-H||=o(1), so a two-stage ladder o(1) -> nu_H > 0 -> O(t^{-1/2}log) -> nu_H closes), but nothing in the paper says so, and the theorem statement bundles the unconditional and conditional halves together. Separately, the emphasised claim that the ridge bound holds "for all t almost surely" / "for **every** t rather than eventually" (appendix l.85-86) is itself circular through the auto-scaling: iota_n = c_iota varsigma_n n^{-varrho} with varsigma_n = d/tr(W_n A_n^{-1}) is an implicit equation (iota_n sits inside A_n; the code, src/bgsn/_core.py l.264-269, uses the pre-update A^{-1} instead), and bootstrapping from the ridge alone does not close: lambda_min(Hbar) >~ n^{-s} gives varsigma_n >~ n^{-s}, hence iota_n >~ n^{-s-varrho} and only lambda_min >~ n^{-s-varrho}, a strictly weaker bound at each pass. The n^{-varrho} floor in fact comes from lambda_min(H) > 0 via the PSD Y-terms, which holds only eventually and with a random constant — i.e. exactly the 'eventually' the paper claims to avoid.
findings.fix: Split thm:curv into (a) an unconditional lemma giving lambda_min(Hbar_t) >= c n_t^{-varrho} and ||Hbar_t^{-1}|| = O(t^{varrho}) (with the constant allowed to be random, and honest about which part is 'for all t' and which is eventual), and (b) a conditional rate statement; then state the bootstrap ladder explicitly as a numbered induction (o(1) -> nu_H^{(1)} -> rate -> nu_H) before thm:as. Define varsigma_n = d/tr(W_{n-1}A_{n-1}^{-1}) to match the implementation and remove the implicit equation.

findings.where: paper/sec_appendix.tex, proof of prop:gap, l.288-297 (and prop:gap statement, main.tex l.568-579)
findings.claim: The Bernoulli-thinning variance is computed as if Y were centred: the diagonal term is written "sum_i p Gamma_0^H", but Var(Z_i Y_i) = p Gamma_0^H + p(1-p) vec(H) vec(H)^T because E[Y_i] = H != 0. The omitted term is Theta(1) and therefore swamps the claimed O(1/m) excess, so the stated formula is false for the estimator defined in the proof.
findings.why: With Hhat^Bern = (pN)^{-1} sum_i Z_i Y_i, the correct answer is n Var[Hhat^Bern] = Gamma_0^H + (1-p) vec(H)vec(H)^T + m^{-1}(S^H - Gamma_0^H) + o(1). Counterexample: let Y_i == H be deterministic, so Gamma^H_k = 0 for all k and the paper's formula gives n Var = 0; but Hhat^Bern = (sum_i Z_i / pN) H has n Var = (1-p) vec(H)vec(H)^T != 0. I verified this numerically (d=2, N=20000, p=0.1, 20000 replicates): the empirical n Var matches (1-p)vec(H)vec(H)^T to three digits, and the paper's prediction is the zero matrix. Since the omitted term does not shrink in m while the advertised Bernoulli penalty is (kappa_H-1)/m, the head-to-head comparison with gapping's O(rho^m) — contribution T5 and prop:gap's entire content — is not established by this proof. Note also that the implementation compares a *self-normalised* estimator (src/bgsn/_core.py normalises by the realised weight W; experiments/exp4_gapping.py forms np.linalg.inv(W*Ainv)), so the proof does not analyse the estimator that is actually run or that the algorithm would use.
findings.fix: Define Hhat^Bern with the realised normaliser, Hhat^Bern = (sum_i Z_i)^{-1} sum_i Z_i Y_i, as the algorithm does, and redo the variance by the delta method for a ratio (the mean-induced term then enters only at second order, restoring Gamma_0^H + m^{-1}(S^H-Gamma_0^H) + o(1)); state the normalisation in the proposition. If the (pN)^{-1} version is kept, the (1-p)vec(H)vec(H)^T term must appear in the statement, and the claimed advantage of gapping re-examined.

findings.where: paper/main.tex thm:lrv (l.517-538, esp. l.531-535) and paper/sec_appendix.tex drift paragraph, l.244-267; cf. thm:as l.416 "for every fixed block length b>=1"
findings.claim: thm:lrv's drift term tau_{b,N} rests on E||delta_{t-1}||^2 = O(log t/(bt)), a *moment* bound that is nowhere established (thm:rate is a purely almost-sure statement with an unspecified random constant), and it is invoked in a regime (b = b_N -> infinity) in which thm:rate/thm:curv are not proved at all.
findings.why: The proof states "on the retained window t ~ T, thm:rate gives E||delta_{t-1}||^2 = O(log t/(bt))". thm:rate says only "||theta_t-theta*||^2 = O(log(N_t)/N_t) almost surely"; an a.s. big-O gives no bound on the expectation without uniform integrability, which is never argued (and the available moment assumptions, as:mom with E||g||^{2+2eta} and as:mix with 2+nu, are weak). Since tau_{b,N} enters claims (i), (ii) and (iv), the bias statements of thm:lrv are unproved. Compounding this, thm:as is stated "for every **fixed** block length b>=1" and thm:curv/thm:rate are a.s. statements along one infinite trajectory at fixed (b,m), whereas thm:lrv assumes "b=b_N -> infinity with b_N=o(N)" and its final sentence invokes thm:clt to conclude the studentised limit and "asymptotically exact coverage" at b ~ log N. With b growing, the recursion itself changes with N: the object is a triangular array, a.s. rates along a fixed trajectory cannot be transferred, and o(T^{-1/2}) is not o(N^{-1/2}) since T^{-1/2} = sqrt(b) N^{-1/2}. The paper's headline inference statement (T2's calibrated intervals) is therefore never proved in the regime in which it is used.
findings.fix: Add an L^2 rate theorem (E||delta_t||^2 = O(log N_t / N_t)) alongside the a.s. rate — this is what the drift analysis needs — and restate thm:as/thm:rate/thm:curv/thm:clt uniformly in b over the range b <= C log N (triangular-array form, with every remainder bound carrying its b-dependence explicitly, e.g. (A),(B) = O(b^{-1/2}T^{-1/2-nu_H} log^{1/2+eps} T)). Alternatively confine thm:lrv to fixed b and prove the coverage claim only for a fixed b chosen large enough that rho^b is negligible.

findings.where: paper/main.tex thm:lrv (iii)-(iv), l.524-529; proof in paper/sec_appendix.tex l.239-242 and l.269-272; cf. term (C) l.175
findings.claim: The operator-norm rate in (iv) does not follow from the entrywise variance in (iii) — the conversion costs a factor d, and the theorem's own side condition betrays this — and the variance bound invokes fourth moments that no assumption provides.
findings.why: (iii) gives Var[Shat^FT_{jk}] = O(b/N) entrywise; the Frobenius bound then yields ||Shat^FT - S||_op = O_p(d sqrt(b/N)), and even under matrix-concentration conditions the best available is O_p(sqrt(db/N)). Yet (iv) states ||Shat^FT-S|| = O_p(sqrt(b/N)+rho^b+tau) "which for b ~ log N and **d = o(sqrt(N/log N))** gives O_p(sqrt(log N/N))". The stated side condition is precisely d*sqrt(log N/N) = o(1), i.e. it buys *consistency* with a d factor present — so the theorem simultaneously assumes the d factor and omits it from the rate. Consequently the Otilde(N^{-1/2}) headline (abstract l.85-86, contribution 2) is proved only for fixed d, not in the d-growing regime the theorem advertises. Independently, the proof of (iii) reads "as:mix plus **fourth moments** give Var[Shat^BM_{jk}] = O(1/T')", but as:mix supplies only E||g_1||^{2+nu} and as:mom only E||g(theta)||^{2+2eta} for *some* eta>0; E||g||^4 < infinity is nowhere assumed, and the variance of a quadratic form in g cannot be bounded without it. Finally, the d-dependence of the curvature fluctuation is handled inconsistently and its justification is not a derivation: thm:lrv asserts E||Hhat_t delta||^2 <~ (1+Cd/b)||H delta||^2 "for delta independent of block t" with the parenthetical "whose trace contributes a factor tr(HM)/b", while the CLT proof (l.175) uses E||Hhat_t-H||^2 = O(1/b) with no d. Under as:curv (E||alpha Phi Phi^T||_op^{eta'} <= C_{eta'}, dimension-free) the correct bound is O(1/b), so the d/b term — and with it the "we do not recommend b << d" reading of tau_{b,N} — presupposes a trace-type/growing-||Phi||^2 scaling that contradicts as:curv; and delta_{t-1} is not independent of block t under mixing, which is the case actually needed.
findings.fix: State (iv) as ||Shat^FT-S||_op = O_p(d sqrt(b/N) + rho^b + tau_{b,N}) (or prove a matrix-Bernstein version giving sqrt(db/N) under an explicit sub-exponential condition) and keep the rate claim to fixed d, or add the d factor to the abstract's Otilde(N^{-1/2}). Add an explicit fourth-moment assumption (E||g(theta)||^4 <= C(1+F(theta)-F(theta*))^2, i.e. eta>=1 in as:mom) and cite it in (iii). Reconcile the curvature-fluctuation bound: either add a trace-scaling assumption that makes d/b real, or drop d from tau_{b,N} and from the b>>d recommendation, and prove the bound for delta_{t-1} dependent on the block (mixing remainder included).

findings.where: paper/sec_appendix.tex, proof of thm:as, l.128-137 (final three lines) and l.130 ("on the event {sup_t ||theta_t||<infinity}")
findings.claim: thm:as claims global almost-sure convergence theta_t -> theta*, but the assumptions contain no convexity or unique-stationary-point condition, the Robbins–Siegmund step is over-read, the justification given for the divergence condition is the wrong inequality, and the boundedness event is assumed rather than proved.
findings.why: Three separate holes in six lines. (1) "Robbins--Siegmund then gives F(theta_t) -> F(theta*) a.s." — the recursion in eq:desc yields only that F(theta_t)-F(theta*) *converges* (to a possibly positive limit) and that sum_t gamma_t grad F' P grad F < infinity; concluding the limit is 0, and then theta_t -> theta*, needs F to have a unique stationary point (or global strong convexity / a Robbins–Monro angle condition). as:reg assumes only ||nabla^2 F|| <= L, H = nabla^2F(theta*) > 0 and local Lipschitzness — nothing rules out other stationary points, and "local strong convexity gives theta_t -> theta*" only converts convergence of F to convergence of theta *inside* the neighbourhood. (2) "since sum_t gamma_t lambda_min(P_{t-1}) = sum_t O(t^{-1}) c = infinity **by the ridge bound**": lambda_min(P_{t-1}) = 1/lambda_max(Hbar_{t-1}), so this needs an *upper* bound on lambda_max(Hbar_t); the ridge gives lambda_min(Hbar_t) >= c n_t^{-varrho}, i.e. an upper bound on ||P||, the opposite direction. lambda_max(Hbar_t) = O(1) a.s. requires the strong law for the Y-terms plus control of term (iv), i.e. the very thing under construction. (3) The whole cross-term argument is run "on the event {sup_t ||theta_t||<infinity}", but that event is what Robbins–Siegmund is supposed to deliver; as used, boundedness is assumed to prove boundedness.
findings.fix: Add an assumption making theta* the unique stationary point (F convex, or inf_{||theta-theta*||>=eps} <grad F(theta), theta-theta*> > 0), and cite it where 'local strong convexity' is invoked; the experiments are all convex M-estimation (sec_limits l.56) so this costs nothing. Replace the 'ridge bound' justification with an explicit a.s. bound lambda_max(Hbar_t) <= lambda_max(H) + o(1) (proved from terms (i)-(iv)). Restructure the localisation so that the stopped/localised process is analysed on {sup_{s<=t}||theta_s||<=K} and boundedness is a *conclusion* of Robbins–Siegmund applied to the localised recursion, with K -> infinity.

findings.where: paper/main.tex l.520 and l.187/496-497; paper/sec_appendix.tex eq:bmbias l.211-216 and l.236-237
findings.claim: Two bookkeeping errors in the long-run-variance algebra: Delta = 2 sum_{k>=1} k Gamma_k is the wrong (asymmetric) object for the batch-means bias, and Shat^FT as defined in eq:Sft is *not* algebraically identical to 2 Shat^BM(2b) - Shat^BM(b).
findings.why: (1) The bias term comes from (1/b) sum_{|k|<b} |k| Gamma_k = (1/b) sum_{k>=1} k(Gamma_k + Gamma_{-k}) = (1/b) sum_{k>=1} k(Gamma_k + Gamma_k^T). The paper's Delta = 2 sum_{k>=1} k Gamma_k equals this only when Gamma_k is symmetric, which fails for d>1 (Gamma_{-k} = Gamma_k^T); as defined, Delta is asymmetric while E[Shat^BM] is symmetric by construction, so claim (i) of thm:lrv is dimensionally wrong for d>1 (the AR designs have symmetric Gamma_k, so the experiments cannot detect it — the same wrong Delta appears in the src/bgsn/_core.py docstring for _finish_lrv). (2) eq:Sft defines Lambdahat_1 over *all* T'-1 consecutive pairs with normaliser 1/(T'-1) (and the implementation does the same, _core.py crs_cur accumulates every consecutive pair), whereas 2Shat^BM(2b)-Shat^BM(b) uses only the T'/2 disjoint odd-even pairs. I checked numerically on a random T=8, b=3, d=2 example: the two matrices differ by 0.58 in max-abs while S itself is O(1). They agree only *in expectation*. Main text asserts "it is algebraically identical to 2 Shat^BM(2b) - Shat^BM(b)", and the appendix quietly inserts "(using disjoint pairs)" — a different estimator from the one defined, implemented and analysed. Also, eq:bmbias's remainders are bounded as "O(b rho^b)" and then reported as "O(rho^b)" one line later.
findings.fix: Define Delta = sum_{k>=1} k (Gamma_k + Gamma_k^T) (and fix the docstring). Change "algebraically identical" to "equal in expectation to 2 Shat^BM(2b) - Shat^BM(b), and identical to it if the disjoint-pair version of Lambdahat_1 is used", or switch eq:Sft and the code to disjoint pairs. Absorb the b factor by stating remainders as O(rho_1^b) for any rho_1 in (rho,1), or keep O(b rho^b) throughout.

findings.claim: The paper simultaneously claims the block length "need not grow with $N$" and assumes $b=b_N\to\infty$; and the two results the interval rests on are stated for incompatible $b$ regimes.
findings.why: Fig. 2's caption ends "This is why our block length need not grow with $N$ (\Cref{rem:whyfast})", but Theorem 7 opens "let $b=b_N\to\infty$ with $b_N=o(\sqrt N)$", and its rate needs $b\asymp\log N$ — which does grow with $N$. Worse, Theorem 2 is stated "for every fixed block length $b\ge1$" and Theorem 3 (rate) "Under the assumptions of \Cref{thm:as}", i.e. fixed $b$ only; yet Theorem 4 is asserted "for $b$ fixed or growing with $b=b_N=o(\sqrt N)$" and Theorem 7's drift step invokes the fixed-$b$ rate theorem verbatim (sec_appendix.tex:248: "on the retained window $t\asymp T$, \Cref{thm:rate} gives $\E\norm{\delta_{t-1}}^2=O(\log t/(bt))$"). So no stated theorem covers the regime in which the headline claim "the intervals above have asymptotically exact coverage" (main.tex:559-560) is actually used. A referee will read the caption as a stronger claim than the theory supports and then find the regimes do not overlap.
findings.fix: (1) Restate Theorems 2 and 3 for $b=b_N$ with the constants uniform over $b_N=o(\sqrt N)$ (the proofs appear to be uniform in $b$ — say so explicitly, e.g. "all bounds below hold uniformly over $b\le\sqrt N$"). (2) Delete "need not grow with $N$" from the Fig. 2 caption and from any similar phrasing; write instead "this is why $b\asymp\log N$ suffices, instead of the $b\asymp N^{3/4}$ that iterate-based batch means need". (3) In §2.1, state once whether $b$ is a constant or a sequence $b_N$, and use $b_N$ consistently in every theorem that lets it grow.

findings.claim: The theorem chain is circular as written: Theorem 1 assumes the conclusion of Theorem 3, Theorem 2's proof invokes Theorem 1, and Theorem 3's proof invokes both — and the paper never states the proof order.
findings.why:
Theorem 1 reads "suppose $	heta_t	o	s$ almost surely with $
orm{	heta_t-	s}=O(t^{-1/2}\log^{c}t)$ a.s.", which is exactly what Theorem 3 delivers ($
orm{	heta_t-	s}^2=O(\log N_t/N_t)$). The proof of Theorem 2 then says "The last term is summable: $\gamma_t^2\opnorm{P_{t-1}}^2=O(t^{2\varrho-2})$ by \Cref{thm:curv}", and Term (A)/(B) of the rate proof again use "By \Cref{thm:curv}". A reader following the appendix in order cannot tell what is assumed and what is proved. The material for a non-circular staging is already there — the appendix notes that the ridge bound holds "for all $t$" from term (ii) alone, and Term (B) mentions "Bootstrapping from $
orm{\delta_t}=o(1)$" — but it is never stated as a logical order.
findings.fix: Split Theorem 1 into (1a) an unconditional statement: $\lambda_{\min}(\Hb_t)\ge c_1n_t^{-\varrho}$ and $\opnorm{\Hb_t^{-1}}=O(t^{\varrho})$ for all $t$ a.s., proved from the ridge alone; and (1b) the conditional rate $\opnorm{\Hb_t-H}=O(t^{-\nu_H})$ given a preliminary rate. Then add one sentence at the head of Appendix A: "The results are proved in the order 1a $\Rightarrow$ Theorem 2 $\Rightarrow$ preliminary rate $O(t^{-1/2}\log^{1/2+\eps}t)$ $\Rightarrow$ 1b $\Rightarrow$ Theorems 3-4", and cite 1a (not Theorem 1) in the proof of Theorem 2.

findings.claim: The paper's one new assumption rests on an undefined quantity, and roughly a dozen terms are used well before (or never) being defined — the abstract alone uses five.
findings.why: Assumption 4 reads "strongly ($\alpha$-)mixing with $\alpha_{\mathrm{mix}}(k)\le K\varrho_0^{\,k}$", but $\alpha_{\mathrm{mix}}$ is never defined anywhere in the paper (it recurs at main.tex:386 and sec_appendix.tex:24,95); a non-specialist cannot check the assumption against their own stream. In the abstract, $H$ and $\Gamma_0$ appear as bare symbols with no gloss, and "sandwich", "score", "batch means", "mixing" and "a single variance-inflation factor $\kappa$" are used with no explanation ($\kappa$ is only defined in §3.4, and there as a per-coordinate ratio $\kappa_j$). "$M$-estimator" (main.tex:147) is never defined. "an offline HAC reference" (sec_experiments.tex:25) never expands HAC. "random scaling" and "plug-in" are first used in the §5 method list but explained only later (sec_related.tex:38) or only in the appendix (sec_appendix_exp.tex:72). "lugsail" is named four times and never explained, and §4 explains "flat-top" using two further undefined terms, "lag-window estimator" and "Richardson extrapolation". "studentised" (sec_appendix.tex:197) and "pivot" (sec_appendix_exp.tex:80) are undefined.
findings.fix: Add a short "Terminology" paragraph at the end of §2 defining, in one line each: $\alpha_{\mathrm{mix}}(k)=\sup\{|\Prob(A\cap B)-\Prob(A)\Prob(B)|\}$ over $A\in\sigma(\xi_i,i\le0)$, $B\in\sigma(\xi_i,i\ge k)$; score; sandwich (instantaneous vs long-run); batch means; $M$-estimator. In the abstract, write "Hessian $H=\nabla^2F$ at the truth" and "lag-0 score covariance $\Gamma_0$", and define $\kappa$ as "the ratio of the correct to the assumed variance". Expand HAC at first use, and add half-line glosses for plug-in, random scaling, studentised, lugsail, lag-window at their first (main-text) occurrence.

findings.claim: Six symbols carry two or three unrelated meanings, including three that appear in theorem statements: $\varrho/\varrho_0/\rho$, $\eps$, $\Phi$, $M$, $s$, $W$.
findings.why:
$\varrho\in(0,1/2)$ is the ridge exponent (main.tex:285) while $\varrho_0$ is the mixing base (main.tex:360) and $ho=\varrho_0^{
u/(2+
u)}$ the autocovariance decay (main.tex:375) — three near-identical glyphs for a tuning knob and two dependence rates. Theorem 1's "for every $
u_H<\min\{\varrho,1/2\}$" therefore reads as a mixing condition, and the $\min$ is vacuous because $\varrho<1/2$ by construction; correspondingly the appendix branch "(and $O(\log^{1/2+\eps}T)$ if $
u_H>1/2$)" (sec_appendix.tex:165) is unreachable. $\eps_t$ is the block score (main.tex:272), $\eps$ is the arbitrary exponent in $\log^{1/2+\eps}$ (sec_appendix.tex:38ff), and $\eps_t$ is a standard-normal innovation in AR-hom (sec_appendix_exp.tex:14-16). $\Phi$ is the normal CDF (main.tex:251), the rank-one curvature factor $\Phi(	heta;\xi)$ (Assumption 3), and the AR matrix $\Phi=\mathrm{diag}(\phi_1,\dots,\phi_d)$ (sec_appendix_exp.tex:21) — with two of the three meanings inside one appendix line, "$e_t=\mathrm{logit}(\Phi(
u_t))$". $M$ is a random orthogonal matrix, $\psi\Phi(I-\psi\Phi)^{-1}$, a generic matrix in the drift bound, and the partial sum $M_T$. $s$ is a Markov state, $x^{\!	op}	s$, and the score $s_i(	heta)$ (the paper's score is $g_i$). $W$ is the curvature weight and the Wiener process $W(1),W(r)$. Separately, main.tex:557 and sec_appendix.tex:251 apply the operator norm to a vector: "$\E\opnorm{\widehat H_t\delta}^2\lesssim(1+d/b)\opnorm{H\delta}^2$".
findings.fix: Rename the ridge exponent (e.g. $q\in(0,1/2)$) and drop the vacuous $\min\{\cdot,1/2\}$ and the dead $\nu_H>1/2$ branch; use $\zeta$/$\varsigma$ for design innovations and reserve $\eps_t$ for the block score; rename the AR coefficient matrix ($A_\phi$) and the orthogonal matrix ($Q$); use $g_i$ for the score in sec_appendix_exp.tex:73; rename the Wiener process ($B$/$W^\circ$) or the accumulator weight; replace $\opnorm{\cdot}$ by $\norm{\cdot}$ wherever the argument is a vector.

findings.claim: Figure 3 — the only measurement of the headline rate — is never referenced and its caption states no number; and several captions are not self-contained (no axes, a term that exists nowhere else, panel letters the reader cannot resolve).
findings.why: In a fresh 3-pass build, "Figure 3" occurs only in its own caption: no \Cref{fig:lrvrate} exists anywhere in main.tex or sec_experiments.tex, so the figure that measures the $\widetilde O(N^{-1/2})$ rate (the paper's second headline claim) is orphaned, and its caption reports no value — "attains the fitted exponent shown, close to the $-1/2$ of \Cref{thm:lrv}(iv)". Fig. 2's caption says the drift contribution is "growing like $(b+d)/N$" while §5.2 says the same quantity "shrinks like $b/N$" (sec_experiments.tex:62) — a reader must re-read to see which. No caption names its axes or scales: Fig. 5's "Slopes are fitted on the four largest $d$" never says time-vs-$d$ on log-log; Fig. 4's "excess" is never given as a formula; Fig. 1(a)'s "as the dependence strength varies" never says the swept quantity is $\phi=\psi$ nor the range. Fig. 7's caption invents "the free block-adequacy diagnostic", a phrase that appears nowhere else in the paper (the text calls it "the free diagnostic $r_j$", defined two pages later). Fig. 6's caption covers panels (a)-(c) while §5.4 discusses (a)-(g), so a reader cannot tell that (d)-(g) are table rows.
findings.fix: Cite Figure 3 in §5.2 and put the fitted exponent in its caption as a macro; make Fig. 2's caption and §5.2 use the same wording for the drift term ($\tau_{b,N}=(b+d)\log^2N/N$); in each caption name the axes, units and scale ("wall-clock seconds vs $d$, log-log"); write "the diagnostic $r_j$ of §5.6" instead of "block-adequacy diagnostic"; and either move (d)-(g) into the figure or say in §5.4 that (d)-(g) are rows of Table X. Note for the team: paper/main.pdf and notes/paper_draft.txt are stale builds — the "Theorem 9/10" for Lemmas and the off-by-one figure references visible there are gone in a fresh build and are not source defects.

findings.claim: The corrected nominal level for Protocol B is stated in terms of an undefined symbol $R$, which also collides with the Markov design's $R$, and its derivation appears nowhere.
findings.why: "the correct nominal level for the comparison is $2\Phi(z_{0.025}/\sqrt{1-1/R})-1$, which we compute exactly and report in the table header" — $R$ is never defined in the paper, and $R$ is separately used for $R=V\mathrm{diag}(\pi)\{\psi P(I-\psi P)^{-1}\}V^{\!\top}$ in Appendix B.1. Protocol B is one of only two real-data protocols and its whole validity rests on this correction; as written the reader can neither reconstruct nor check it. The limitations section compounds this by asserting "we correct the nominal level for that exactly, but the correction assumes the segments are approximately exchangeable" without ever showing the correction.
findings.fix: Define $R$ at first use (e.g. "$R=N_{\text{full}}/N_{\text{segment}}$, the number of segments the full-stream target is built from") and give the one-line derivation, $\Var(\hat\theta_{\text{seg}}-\hat\theta_{\text{full}})=(1-1/R)\Var(\hat\theta_{\text{seg}})$ under the stated exchangeability, in a footnote or Appendix B; rename either this $R$ or the Markov-design $R$.

findings.claim: Five sentences will force a competent non-specialist to re-read; two of them also introduce an undefined symbol or a notational error.
findings.why: (1) main.tex:412-415: "Two routes are available---a Poisson-equation/martingale decomposition, or a direct maximal inequality for mixing sums---and we take the second, because the object that actually has to be controlled is the weighted series $\sum_t\gamma_t\Hb_{t-1}^{-1}\eps_t$, and for that the conditional-bias route is lossy." Three undefined notions in one sentence ("Poisson equation", "conditional-bias route", "lossy"). (2) main.tex:555-558: the $\tau_{b,N}$ sentence is 60+ words with two nested causal clauses and applies $\opnorm{\cdot}$ to a vector. (3) main.tex:311-315: "leaves a component that decays like $t^{-c}$ with $c<1$" — $c$ is undefined here and already means four other things ($\log^c t$ in Thm 1, the eigenvalue exponent in $\Sigma$, $c_\iota$, $c_{\mathrm w}$). (4) main.tex:534-538: "keep two accumulators covering the current and previous dyadic windows $[2^{k},2^{k+1})$ and report from their union, so at any time at least half and at most three quarters of the blocks are retained" — $k$ is never tied to $T'$ and the 1/2-3/4 claim is unexplained. (5) sec_experiments.tex:45-47: "replacing only the variance estimator repairs the base method ... this isolates the inference component as the operative one" — "repairs" (coverage? width?) and "the operative one" are both left to the reader.
findings.fix: (1) "Under dependence $\E[\eps_t\mid\Fil_{t-1}]\neq0$, so the martingale argument used under independence is unavailable. One could remove the conditional bias via a Poisson equation; we instead bound the weighted sum $\sum_t\gamma_t\Hb_{t-1}^{-1}\eps_t$ directly with a maximal inequality for mixing sums (Lemma 10), which gives a sharper bound on exactly the object we need." (2) Split into three sentences, one per source of error, and use $\norm{\cdot}$ for vectors. (3) Name the exponent: "decays like $t^{-c}$ where $c=\lambda_{\min}(\Hb^{-1}H)<1$ while the preconditioner is poor". (4) "At block $T'$ set $k=\lfloor\log_2T'\rfloor$; we keep one accumulator over blocks $[2^{k-1},2^{k})$ and one over $[2^{k},T']$ and report their sum, so the retained set is always a suffix holding between $1/2$ and $3/4$ of the blocks and the discarded prefix is exactly the early, high-drift blocks." (5) "Coverage is restored when the base method's iterates are combined with our long-run variance, and is not restored when our iterates are combined with the i.i.d. plug-in variance: the variance estimator, not the point estimator, is what fixes coverage."

findings.claim: The thesis arrives at word 118 of a 327-word abstract, the contribution list sprawls to six items of which the paper itself downgrades two, and the same disclaimer is made three times; the abstract's numbers also sit outside the anti-drift mechanism the paper advertises.
findings.why: The abstract spends its first 117 words on background before "We show that a streaming quasi-Newton method can be made valid on dependent streams". Of the six contributions, #4 is described in the body as "The proof is one line" and "textbook geometric summation" (main.tex:480) and #5 is disclaimed in §7 as "the end-to-end effect ... is second order and we could not measure it reliably" (sec_limits.tex:66-70) — so a referee will ask why they are numbered contributions at all, diluting the single defensible message. The boundary disclaimers appear three separate times ("What we do not claim" in §1, the prior-art paragraphs in §6, "One thing we deliberately do not claim" in §7), costing about a page. Finally, §5 opens "Every number quoted below is generated from the saved results ... so the prose cannot drift from the data", but the abstract's "68--75\%", "94--95\%", "1.3$\times$", "0.9$\times$" are hard-coded, and the corresponding experiment output (results/exp1_main.json) does not yet exist, so the abstract is currently outside that guarantee.
findings.fix: Compress the abstract's opening to one sentence and state the thesis by word 40 ("Streaming quasi-Newton estimators are asymptotically efficient at first-order cost, but on dependent streams their stated uncertainty is wrong by a fixed factor; we show one structural change fixes both the estimate and the interval within the same $O(dN)$ budget"). Demote Propositions 6 and 8 to remarks, or merge contributions 4-5 into one "two small companions" item, leaving three headline claims. Keep the boundary discussion in §7 only, with a one-line pointer from §1. Make the abstract's four numbers macros from the same results file as the body.

findings.where: src/bgsn/realdata.py:131-159 (`conditional_oracle`) + src/bgsn/streams.py:50-54 (`sandwich_true`) + experiments/exp6_real.py:69,121 (`H_true=orc.H`, `H_true=empirical_hessian(...)`); affects every Protocol A/B metro number in \Cref{tab:real}
findings.claim: Four of the ten metro segments used by Protocols A and B have an exactly rank-deficient design, so the "exact conditional oracle" is the inverse of a singular matrix.
findings.why: `_standardise` standardises over the full stream, so within a 4000-hour segment a feature can be constant. I checked: segments 0, 6, 7, 8 have `log_rain` identically constant (no recorded rain in the window), i.e. exactly collinear with the intercept. Measured cond(X_s'X_s/n) = 2.96e16, 2.39e16, 3.73e17, 2.03e16 (min eigenvalue 2.9e-16, 2.7e-17, 2.4e-16, -2.7e-17) against 45.6 for the full stream. `conditional_oracle` returns that H, and `Oracle.sandwich_true` does `np.linalg.inv(self.H)`; the same singular H is handed to ASGD/AdaGrad through `_sandwich_from_H`. So on 40% of the metro segments kappa, the infeasible-oracle interval, `width_rel`, `rmse_rel` (which divides by V) and the first-order baselines' standard errors are numerical noise, and one of the twelve coordinates is not even identified inside the segment. The prose calls this protocol "an *exact* target and an exact conditional long-run covariance" (paper/sec_experiments.tex:120-121).
findings.fix: Detect and drop (or ridge/pseudo-invert with a reported rank) degenerate columns per segment, or choose segment boundaries/features so every segment has full rank; report per-segment cond(H) in the appendix and re-run Protocol A and B for metro. Do not average coverage/rmse over segments whose oracle is singular.

findings.where: src/bgsn/_core.py:244-250 (plug-in accumulation) sits *before* the `if warm: ... continue` at :259-273; used by `BGSN-plugin` and `SN-iid` in experiments/common.py:56-60,92-94
findings.claim: The i.i.d. plug-in $\Gz$ — the variance of the dependence-blind competitor that the whole paper is benchmarked against — accumulates scores over the curvature warm-up blocks, where $\theta$ is still $\theta_0=0$, so on real data it is inflated by three orders of magnitude.
findings.why: During warm-up no parameter step is taken, so $c_i=x_i^\top 0-y_i=-y_i$. On the real-data configuration ($n=4000$, $b=40$, $d=12$) `n_warm = ceil(50*12/40) = 15` blocks $=600$ observations $=15\%$ of every segment, and $y=\log(\text{volume})\approx 7.8$ while the residual scale is $0.45$. I ran the exact Protocol A configuration on metro segment 0: median over coordinates of $\mathrm{diag}(\Gz)/\mathrm{diag}(\Gamma_0^{\text{true}}) = 1171$, i.e. the dependence-blind standard errors are $\approx 34\times$ too large (per-coordinate ratios 34.6, 18.8, 34.6, 31.2, 35.4, 33.8). The quantities \RealCovPluginMetroA/\RealCovPluginAirqA quoted at paper/sec_experiments.tex:122 as "the dependence-blind interval covers ..." therefore do not measure a dependence-blind interval at all; the same contamination hits the `SN-iid` row (same kernel, same `warm_mult=50` default). On the simulated designs the effect is ~1% ($n_{\text{warm}}b/N=0.5\%$, $\E[y^2]/\E[u^2]\approx3.4$), still a systematic upward shift of the measured plug-in coverage that the "exact within Monte Carlo error" claim of \Cref{prop:coverage} (sec_experiments.tex:32-34) cannot absorb.
findings.fix: Move the `want_plugin` accumulation after the `if warm: ... continue` (or, better, evaluate $\Gz$ at the final iterate, as is already done for `empirical_hessian`/`offline_hac`), state in \Cref{app:hyper} at which $\theta$ $\Gz$ is evaluated, and re-run every table that contains a `-plugin` or `SN-iid` row.

findings.claim: The paper's own saved results contradict both bias claims at the small-$b$ end: "Plain batch means track the closed-form prediction $1-\Delta/(bS)$ over the whole range" and "the two-scale estimator is unbiased at every $b$".
findings.why: At $b=5$, `bm_alg` $=0.74874\pm0.00078$ against `theory_bm` $=0.74207$ — a $8.5\sigma$ discrepancy. It is not Monte Carlo noise: the exact finite-$b$ expectation $\sum_{|k|<b}(1-|k|/b)\Gamma_k/S=[1+2\sum_{k=1}^{4}(1-k/5)0.49^k]/2.9216=0.74936$ matches the measurement to $0.8\sigma$, so what fails is the paper's dropped $O(\rho^b)$ term, exactly at the $b$ where the paper's whole point ($b\asymp\log N$) lives. Likewise `ft_alg` $=0.99238\pm0.00119$ at $b=5$ is $6.4\sigma$ below $1$. "This is \Cref{thm:lrv}(i)--(ii) with no fitted constants" (line 54-55) is thus refuted at the first plotted point in \Cref{fig:lrv}(a). Relatedly, `ft_drift` is 0.00100, 0.00081, 0.00098, 0.00148, 0.00253, 0.00448, 0.00882 for $b=5..320$ — non-monotone at small $b$ and ~10x larger than $b/N$, so "shrinks like $b/N$" (line 62-63) is both mis-signed in words (it *grows* in $b$ at fixed $N$) and unverified in constant.
findings.fix: Plot the exact expectation $\sum_{|k|<b}(1-|k|/b)\Gamma_k$ as the theory curve (it is closed form for this design), restrict the "tracks/unbiased" wording to $b\ge10$, and state explicitly that the residual at $b=5$ is the $O(\rho^b)$ term. Rephrase the drift sentence as "is of order $b/N$ and grows with $b$".

findings.claim: The abstract's width factor is wrong and inconsistent with the paper's own exact prediction; and the abstract is the one place where numbers are hardcoded rather than macro-injected.
findings.why: The abstract says intervals "cover $94$--$95\%$ at $1.3\times$ the width", while the body says "our interval is $\WidthRatioArhom\times$ the dependence-blind one, which is exactly $\sqrt{\kappa}$" and \Cref{app:dgps} fixes $\kappa=2.922$ for AR-hom, i.e. $\sqrt{\kappa}=1.71$. The abstract's own coverage range, $68$--$75\%$, inverts to $\kappa\in[2.92,3.88]$ and hence width ratios $1.71$--$1.97$: no design in the paper can give $1.3$. This also breaks the stated no-drift guarantee ("Every number quoted below is generated from the saved results ... so the prose cannot drift from the data", sec_experiments.tex:1-3) — `make_tables.py` emits macros only for the body, and `$68$--$75\%$`, `$94$--$95\%$`, `$1.3\times$`, `$0.9\times$` are literals.
findings.fix: Replace the abstract's literals with macros derived from `facts.json` (e.g. a min/max over designs of `width_ratio` and `time_ratio`) and re-check that the quoted range equals $\sqrt{\kappa}$ over the four designs.

findings.claim: The Protocol B target-uncertainty correction $\Var(\theta_{\text{seg}}-\theta_{\text{full}})=\Var(\theta_{\text{seg}})(1-1/R)$ is not exact and its three assumptions are never stated.
findings.why: The identity holds only if $\theta_{\text{full}}=R^{-1}\sum_k\theta_k$ with the $\theta_k$ independent and equal-variance: then $\Var(\theta_k-\bar\theta)=V[(1-1/R)^2+(R-1)/R^2]=V(1-1/R)$. None of the three holds here. (i) `offline_mestimator` gives the *Hessian-weighted* average $\theta_{\text{full}}=\sum_k W_k\theta_k$, $W_k=(X'X)^{-1}X_k'X_k$; I measured $\lVert W_k-I/R\rVert_F/\lVert I/R\rVert_F$ over the ten metro segments $=0.33,0.34,0.39,0.46,0.47,0.50,0.54,0.58,0.58,0.96$, with $\mathrm{diag}(W_k)$ for `temp` ranging over $[0.063,0.185]$ against $1/R=0.1$. (ii) The segments are adjacent slices of a stream with $\hat\rho_1=0.755$, so they are not independent. (iii) Segment variances differ, and in four metro segments they are singular (see the rank-deficiency finding). Moreover $\theta_{\text{seg}}$ is the *streaming* estimator, not the segment $M$-estimator, so its covariance with $\theta_{\text{full}}$ is not $V/R$. Calling this "which we compute exactly" and printing it as \emph{the} nominal level in the table header (make_tables.py:161-163) overstates what is a first-order approximation.
findings.fix: State the three assumptions in \Cref{app:dgps}; either use the exact weighted formula $\Var(\theta_k-\theta_{\text{full}})=(I-W_k)V_k(I-W_k)^\top+\sum_{l\neq k}W_lV_lW_l^\top$ per coordinate, or make the target a *held-out* estimator computed from segments other than $k$ (then the correction is $1+1/(R-1)$ and needs no equal-weighting assumption), and replace "exactly" with "to first order".

findings.claim: The real-data coverage summaries treat clustered, conditional-on-covariate-path replicates as independent, and the quoted "about a third" prediction is not the quantity the table measures.
findings.why: In `summarise_a` the group for (stream, method) contains $\#\text{segments}\times n_{\text{noise}}=10\times40=400$ records for metro, and the standard error is `covm.mean(axis=1).std(ddof=1)/np.sqrt(len(rs))` — i.e. $\sqrt{400}$. But the 40 noise replicates inside a segment share the same covariate path *and the same conditional oracle*, so segment is a cluster: $\Var(\bar{c})=\sigma_b^2/10+\sigma_w^2/400$, not $(\sigma_b^2+\sigma_w^2)/400$; the reported SE can be understated by up to $\sqrt{40}\approx6\times$. Protocol B has the same defect (clusters = segments). The paper also never says that Protocol A coverage is *conditional on ten fixed covariate paths* rather than an unconditional coverage. Separately, the prose reasons "the estimated variance inflation is around $2$ for traffic and around $20$ for air quality: on the latter a dependence-blind $95\%$ interval would cover about a third of the time", but coverage is pooled over coordinates and $\hat\kappa_j$ is wildly heterogeneous: I measure $\hat\kappa_j\in[0.90,11.07]$ (metro) and $[2.16,62.95]$ (Aotizhongxin). The pooled prediction $d^{-1}\sum_j\{2\Phi(z/\sqrt{\kappa_j})-1\}$ is $0.786$ and $0.430$, not the $0.820$/$0.344$ obtained from the median $\kappa$ — a 9-point gap on air quality. And Protocol A's own $\kappa$ (AR(1) errors at $\psi=0.755$) has per-segment medians $4.5$–$5.9$ on metro, not the "around 2" quoted in the same paragraph.
findings.fix: Report a cluster-robust (segment-level) MC standard error; say explicitly that Protocol A coverage is conditional on the realised covariate segments; and compare the measured pooled coverage to the pooled prediction $d^{-1}\sum_j\{2\Phi(z/\sqrt{\kappa_j})-1\}$, or report per-coordinate min/max as \Cref{tab:main} does.

findings.claim: On real data the first-order baselines are not tuned as the appendix claims: one grid search on metro's first 8000 rows — which are evaluation segments 0 and 1 — supplies the step constants for all twelve air-quality streams as well.
findings.why: The code comment says "crude but fair tuning ... on the first metro segment": `Xp = metro.X[:8000]` with `b=40`, and the resulting `tuned` dict is then passed unchanged to Protocol A/B for `airq` at `n_seg=5000, b=50`. The appendix states baselines are tuned "on eight *pilot* streams whose seeds are disjoint from the evaluation streams" and "separately for every DGP and $N$" (common.py:8-13 repeats this as a fairness rule). Both halves fail here: the tuning window overlaps the evaluation segments (which flatters the baselines), and the constant is transported across datasets whose response scales differ by a factor of two in level ($\log(\text{volume})\approx7.8$ vs $\log(1+\text{PM2.5})\approx4$) and whose $\kappa$ differs by an order of magnitude (which cripples them on the air-quality stream — the stream that carries the paper's strongest real-data claim).
findings.fix: Tune per dataset on a leading hold-out block that is excluded from the evaluation segments, report the selected constants and the grid (as is done for the simulated designs in `results/exp1_main.json`), and confirm the optimum is interior for each stream.

findings.claim: The two repository artefacts the paper offers as verification are both wrong: the random-scaling critical-value script records a value that is neither correct nor the one used, and the test that validates the streaming covariance accumulator fails.
findings.why: (a) `random_scaling_critical_values` simulates the *absolute* pivot $|W(1)|/(\int B^2)^{1/2}$, so the two-sided 95% value is its 0.95 quantile ($6.746$). The script instead prints and saves `used_two_sided_95 = q[0.975] = 8.154` as "the two-sided 95% critical value used throughout", while the experiments in fact use $6.811$. Its cross-check table is also shifted by one level — it prints "q0.95: simulated 6.746 | KVB 5.374" although $5.374$ is the KVB value for the *signed* statistic, whose match is the simulated 0.90 quantile $5.323$; correctly aligned, simulated/published agree to 1%, but as printed the "cross-check" appears to disagree by $\approx1.4$ at every level. Since \Cref{app:hyper} devotes a paragraph to this number "so the number used in the experiments is verifiable from this repository", the artefact must not contradict it. (b) I ran `test_dyadic_window_matches_explicit`: it fails, `rel.err = 1.38e-2` against `atol 1e-10`, because it rebuilds blocks from `X[:T*b]` while the recorded trajectory starts at block `n_warm` (`exp3_lrv.py:44` gets this right with `X[nw*b:(nw+T)*b]`). \Cref{app:dgps} points at this file ("which is checked in \texttt{tests/test\_oracles.py}") and the file claims to hold "the checks a referee would want to see".
findings.fix: Save `used_two_sided_95 = q[0.95]`, compare row $q_{1-\alpha}$ of the absolute pivot against the KVB value for level $1-\alpha/2$ of the signed statistic, and reconcile the printed number with `RS_CRIT95`. Fix the test's block offset to `X[nw*b:(nw+T)*b]` and add it to CI. While there: \Cref{rem:psd} promises a fallback to $u_j^\top\Sbm u_j$, but `_sandwich_se` (estimators.py:52) clamps the variance to $0$ instead, so the described safeguard does not exist; and the "adeq" column of \Cref{tab:ablation} uses $|\mathrm{diag}(\Sft-\Sbm)|/\mathrm{diag}(\Sft)$ (exp5_ablations.py:30-31), not the $r_j=|u_j^\top(\Sft-\Sbm)u_j|/(u_j^\top\Sft u_j)$ defined in the text and used in exp6.

findings.claim: The `b ~ N^{3/4}` arm of the rate experiment is skipped at *every* N, so the series the Figure-7 caption explicitly describes cannot appear; and `exp8_lrv_rate.json` is not a prerequisite of the Makefile `exp` target, so `make all` never produces Figure 7 at all.
findings.why: `SCHEDULES["n34"] = lambda N: max(int(np.ceil(N ** 0.75)), 8)` is filtered by `if b > N // 40: continue`. I evaluated the guard over the whole `NS` list: 25000→b=1989>625, 50000→3344>1250, 100000→5624>2500, 200000→9458>5000, 400000→15906>10000, 800000→26750>20000, 1600000→44988>40000 — every single N is skipped, so `res["n34"]["rows"] == []`, `len(rows) >= 3` fails, and `make_figures.fig7_lrv_rate` silently drops the series via `if name not in res or not res[name]["rows"]: continue`. The caption nevertheless asserts "The $b\asymp N^{3/4}$ schedule that iterate-based batch means require is shown for reference and is much worse here, because it leaves too few blocks." Separately, `exp:` lists only exp0–exp7, so `results/exp8_lrv_rate.json` is never built by `make all` and `_ok()` makes fig7 a "pending" box — i.e. the numerical check of Thm. lrv(iv), the Otilde(N^{-1/2}) rate that Contribution 2 and the abstract's "against $N^{-1/8}$" comparison rest on, currently reaches the paper through no figure, table, or macro.
findings.fix: Relax the guard so the N^{3/4} arm survives (e.g. cap `b = min(sched(N), N // 8)` and record the cap, or drop the floor to `N // 8`), add `$(RES)/exp8_lrv_rate.json` to the Makefile `exp` prerequisites, and if the arm is genuinely infeasible delete the sentence about it from the caption rather than letting the figure silently omit it.

findings.claim: The verification script publishes 8.154 as "the two-sided 95% critical value used throughout" — it is the 0.975 quantile of an already-absolute-valued statistic — while the code actually uses 6.811 (common.py:45) / 6.747 (estimators.py:126), and its cross-check against the published table is misaligned by one quantile level so it disagrees at every row even though the sampler is correct.
findings.why: `random_scaling_critical_values` returns quantiles of `np.abs(rng.standard_normal(c)) / denom`, i.e. of |W(1)|/sqrt(int B^2). I confirmed the sampler twice: KL expansion gives {0.90:5.325, 0.95:6.758, 0.975:8.169} and an independent discretised-Brownian-motion simulation gives {0.90:5.323, 0.95:6.754, 0.975:8.156}. The two-sided 95% value is therefore the 0.95 quantile (~6.75), not `q[0.975]`. But line 27-28 prints "two-sided 95% critical value used throughout: {q[0.975]:.3f} (NOT {published[0.95]:.3f}, which is the one-sided 95% quantile)" and line 31 saves `used_two_sided_95=q[0.975]` = 8.1542. Moreover `published = {0.90: 3.890, 0.95: 5.374, 0.975: 6.811, 0.99: 8.544}` are quantiles of the *signed* statistic, so the printed comparison reads "q0.900: simulated 5.323 | KVB(2000)/LLSS Table 2 3.890" etc. — a 25-37% apparent mismatch at every level. sec_appendix_exp.tex:98-101 claims "Our own simulation of that quantile ... gives $6.746$" and that the two agree; the artifact a referee is pointed to asserts a different number and a failed cross-check. The appendix also claims "the sampler is validated by reproducing $\E\int_0^1B^2=1/6$ and $\Var\int_0^1B^2=1/45$" — I grepped the whole repo and no such check exists.
findings.fix: Use `q[0.95]` (and `published[0.975]`) as the two-sided 95% value in exp0; relabel the `published` dict as signed-statistic quantiles and compare `q[level]` against `published[(1+level)/2]`; and either add the E/Var(int B^2) moment checks the appendix advertises or delete that parenthesis.

findings.claim: Gamma0_hat is accumulated over the warm-up blocks, where theta is still frozen at theta_0 = 0, whereas S_bm/S_ft explicitly exclude those blocks — so the dependence-blind competitor's variance is inflated by ~1.7% for purely implementational reasons, shifting the coverage-law check by ~+0.004.
findings.why: The `if want_plugin == 1: ... n_plugin += 1` block sits inside pass 1 of *every* block, before the `if warm: ... continue` that skips the step and the covariance accrual; during warm-up theta never changes, so 50*d observations of score are evaluated at theta_0 = 0. Measured on AR-hom (d=20, N=200k, b=20, c_w=50, 6 seeds): mean diag(H^{-1} Gamma0_hat H^{-1})/truth = 1.0175 +/- 0.0024 as implemented, versus 0.9940 +/- 0.0023 when the warm-up observations are dropped. That +0.9% inflation of the SE moves the dependence-blind coverage from the predicted 2*Phi(z/sqrt(kappa))-1 = 0.7485 to ~0.7526. main.tex:496-498 claims eq.(kappa) makes Prop. coverage "checkable to three decimals", and exp2's headline statistic is `max_abs_error = max |cov_BGSN-plugin - predicted_plugin_coverage|`, quoted as \CovLawMaxErr with sec_experiments.tex:33 asserting "the prediction is exact within Monte Carlo error at every dependence level". A +0.004 systematic offset is the same order as the R=400 Monte Carlo SE, so the three-decimal claim is being tested against a biased estimator.
findings.fix: Guard the plug-in accumulator with the warm-up flag (move it inside the non-warm branch, or `if want_plugin == 1 and not warm:`) so Gamma0_hat and S_ft are computed on the same observations; then re-run exp2 and re-quote \CovLawMaxErr.

findings.claim: Five kappa macros are emitted with a capital K but used with a lowercase k, so they are undefined control sequences and the kappa values are blank in the compiled paper.
findings.why: `emit_macros` builds each name as `"".join(ch for ch in k.title().replace("_", "") if ch.isalpha())`, and `"kappa lo arhom".title()` = "Kappa Lo Arhom" -> `\KappaLoArhom`. The prose uses `$\kappa=\kappaLoArhom$` (line 8), `$[\kappaLoArhet,\kappaHiArhet]$` (line 10) and `$[\kappaLoLogistic,\kappaHiLogistic]$` (line 44). Every other macro matches (\CovBgsnArhom, \LrvDriftAtBTwenty, \RealCovBgsnMetroA, \CovLawMaxErr all round-trip correctly), so this is exactly five broken names. The Makefile `paper` target runs `pdflatex -interaction=nonstopmode ... >/dev/null`, so the errors are swallowed and the numbers simply vanish — visible in the current render, notes/paper_draft.txt:405-406 "the same variance inflation 𝜅 = in every coordinate" and "𝜅 𝑗 ranging over [, ]", and :445 "where 𝜅 ranges over [, ]".
findings.fix: Either rename the three uses in sec_experiments.tex to \KappaLoArhom / \KappaLoArhet / \KappaHiArhet / \KappaLoLogistic / \KappaHiLogistic, or special-case the macro-name builder; and stop redirecting pdflatex output to /dev/null so undefined-control-sequence errors are not silently absorbed.

findings.claim: Equation (eq:Sft) defines hat-Lambda_1 with denominator T'-1 over pairs with t, t+1 both in the retained window, but the code divides by T' and includes the pair that straddles the window's left edge (its first block has already been discarded from the batch-means accumulator).
findings.why: The dyadic roll at `if tp == next_pow:` happens *before* the pair accumulation, so the pair (last block of the discarded window, first retained block) is charged to `crs_cur`. Tracing the recursion gives `npair_prev + npair_cur == cnt_prev + cnt_cur == nkeep` exactly, while the nkeep retained blocks contain only nkeep-1 internal pairs. I verified this numerically at d=4, b=5, T_total=37 (n_warm=4, T'=33, nkeep=18): the returned S_ft matches the code's formula (nkeep pairs, one reaching one block before the window) to 3e-16 and differs from eq.(eq:Sft) by 8%; it differs from the 'averaged' variant b(Lam1+Lam1')/2 by 11%, confirming both orientations are correctly *added* not averaged. S_bm itself matches the explicit batch-means computation to 4e-16, and _riccati_vec/_riccati_basis match direct matrix inverses to 6e-18 over 200 accumulated updates, so the algebra is otherwise right. The discrepancy is O(1/T') and therefore ~1e-4 at the experiments' T' ~ 10^4 — but tests/test_oracles.py has now been updated to assert the code's behaviour, so the paper's equation is the side that is out of sync.
findings.fix: Change eq.(eq:Sft) to `hat-Lambda_1 = (1/T') sum_{t: t+1 in T} gbar_t gbar_{t+1}^T` and add half a sentence that the pair straddling the window's left edge is retained (it is stationary, so the expectation is unchanged), or move the roll after the pair accumulation and divide by T'-1.

findings.claim: Protocol A's synthetic error paths are seeded from `hash((name, i0, rep))`, which is salted per process, so every number in Table 3's Protocol A columns and in Fig. 6(c) is irreproducible across runs.
findings.why: `u = RD.ar1_errors(len(X), psi, sg, seed=hash((name, i0, rep)) % (2 ** 31))` — `name` is a Python string, and string hashing has been randomised per interpreter since 3.3 unless PYTHONHASHSEED is fixed. I grepped the whole repo: PYTHONHASHSEED appears nowhere, and `experiments/_env.py` sets only OMP/MKL/OPENBLAS/VECLIB/NUMEXPR thread counts. Because `protocol_a` dispatches through joblib/loky worker *processes*, each worker also has its own salt. sec_appendix_exp.tex claims "\texttt{make all} runs everything" and the paper leans on Protocol A as its one exact-ground-truth real-data result; a referee re-running it will not reproduce the tabulated coverages even bit-for-bit-identical code and data.
findings.fix: Replace with a deterministic seed, e.g. `zlib.crc32(f"{name}|{i0}|{rep}".encode()) % 2**31` or an explicit integer index over (stream, segment, rep).

findings.claim: `andrews_bandwidth` mixes Andrews' alpha(2) numerator with the Bartlett (q=1) constant 1.1447, inflating the bandwidth by up to ~7x; and the function is dead code whose docstring advertises a bandwidth-sensitivity experiment the paper does not contain.
findings.why: Line 212 is `num += 4.0 * rho ** 2 * s2 ** 2 / (1 - rho) ** 8`, but the Bartlett rule `L = 1.1447 * (alpha(1) * n)**(1/3)` (line 217) requires alpha(1) with numerator `4 rho^2 sigma^4 / [(1-rho)^6 (1+rho)^2]`; `(1-rho)^8` is Andrews' alpha(2), used with the quadratic-spectral/Parzen constants. At the built-in cap `rho_cap = 0.9` this overstates alpha(1) by ((1+rho)/(1-rho))^2 = 361 and the bandwidth by 361^(1/3) ~ 7.1x. It is also never exercised: `offline_hac` only calls it when `lag is None`, and every call site passes an explicit lag (common.py:78 `lag=aux.get("hac_lag", 100)`, exp6_real.py:116 `lag=min(500, len(X) // 20)`, exp7_cost.py:81 `lag=100`). The docstring's "We cap the fitted rho ... and always report the value used; the real-data section shows that conclusions do not move over a wide bandwidth range" therefore describes behaviour the repo does not have — the real-data section sweeps the *block* length, not the HAC bandwidth.
findings.fix: Fix the exponent to `(1 - rho) ** 6 * (1 + rho) ** 2`, and either wire the automatic bandwidth into the offline-HAC reference (reporting the selected L, which `extras["lag"]` already carries) or delete the function and the sensitivity claim from its docstring.

findings.claim: The real-data block-length sweep holds the segment length fixed at 4000, so increasing b simultaneously collapses the number of blocks; at the top of the sweep the estimator is built from 5 block gradients and 8 parameter steps, which confounds "b exceeds the dependence horizon" with "T is too small".
findings.why: `protocol_a(..., 4000, b, ...)` with metro d=12 (intercept + temp + log_rain + clouds + 6 calendar harmonics + holiday + weekend). Working the code's own arithmetic (`n_warm = ceil(50*d/b)`, T = 4000/b, dyadic retention keeps blocks [2^{j-1}, T']): b=10 -> T=400, T'=340, nkeep=213; b=40 -> T=100, T'=85, nkeep=54; b=160 -> T=25, T'=21, nkeep=14; b=400 -> T=10, T'=8, nkeep=5. So the 12x12 S_ft at b=400 is estimated from five block gradients (78 free parameters), and only eight 1/t steps are taken. The prose claims "on the traffic stream $r_j$ falls below $0.05$ once $b\ge40$, which is exactly where coverage reaches nominal", and the Fig. 6 caption calls it "the free block-adequacy diagnostic falls below 0.05 exactly where coverage reaches nominal" — but the deterioration at the large-b end is at least as consistent with T -> 0 as with block-length bias, so the alignment is not evidence for the diagnostic.
findings.fix: Hold the number of retained blocks roughly fixed while sweeping b (scale n_seg with b, e.g. n_seg = 200*b), or restrict the sweep to b where nkeep is above some floor (say 50) and state the floor; alternatively report nkeep and T alongside each point so the confound is visible.

reason: Both halves check out against the text. (1) sec_appendix.tex:248-249 asserts "on the retained window t≍T, thm:rate gives E||delta_{t-1}||^2 = O(log t/(bt))", but thm:rate (main.tex:434-438) is purely almost sure with an unspecified random constant. Grepping the whole paper, \E\norm{\delta appears exactly once — in that drift paragraph — so no L^2 rate exists anywhere; lem:series' L^2 half (sec_appendix.tex:49-50) covers only weighted sums of stationary zeta with deterministic weights, not delta_t, and no uniform integrability is argued. Because thm:lrv (i) and (ii) are literally statements about E[Sbar] and E[Shat] carrying O(tau_{b,N}), they cannot be derived from an a.s. rate: the step is invalid as written, not merely loose. notes/base_paper.txt shows the base paper's rates are also a.s./conditional (E[||xi||^2|F_t]=O(t^-rho) a.s.), so this is not fixable by citation. (2) thm:as (main.tex:431) is stated "for every fixed block length b>=1", thm:rate is "under the assumptions of thm:as", thm:curv is a.s. along one trajectory; yet thm:lrv (main.tex:541-542) requires b=b_N->infinity (essential, since rho^b->0 is the mechanism) and invokes thm:rate/thm:curv/thm:clt there. With b=b_N the recursion is a triangular array and Borel-Cantelli-based a.s. rates do not transfer; thm:clt states the growing-b case but its proof (sec_appendix.tex:162-189) is assembled entirely from those fixed-b a.s. bounds. (3) The order mismatch is real: lines 166/171/179 prove (A),(B),(C)=o(T^{-1/2}) while line 183 concludes sqrt(N_T)delta_T = -N_T^{-1/2}H^{-1}sum g_i + o_p(1), which needs o(N_T^{-1/2}) = o(b^{-1/2}T^{-1/2}) — stronger by sqrt(b). Harmless at fixed b, insufficient at b~log N. (4) Nothing in sec_limits.tex addresses it: the "Rates and what we do not prove" paragraph (l.49-57) disclaims only Berry-Esseen and minimax optimality; there is no mention of L^2 rates, uniformity in b, or triangular arrays anywhere in the repo. Downgrading rationale (kept at major, not blocking): the finding's rhetoric that the headline claim "is never proved" overstates the damage. tau_{b,N} is a dominated remainder that changes no reported rate; part (iv), being O_p, nearly survives on a.s. drift bounds; and the repair works with machinery already present — lem:davydov gives sum_k ||Lambda_k|| <= C/b, so (A),(B) in fact carry a spare b^{-1/2} that exactly cancels the sqrt(b) deficit, it is just never written. So the results look true but the written proofs of thm:lrv(i),(ii) and of thm:clt/thm:lrv in the b->infinity regime have genuine gaps that need an added L^2 rate (or a restatement of (i),(ii) as O_p/a.s.) plus explicit b-dependence in every remainder. Note the finding's line pointers are stale (thm:lrv is 539-561, thm:as 429-432); the sec_appendix.tex:244-267 pointer is exact.

REAL, and the core of it is verifiable line-by-line in /Volumes/Crucial X6/MacBook/Code/ml_papers/streaming_qn_dependent/paper/sec_appendix.tex.

1) Hypothesis as stated (l.36-38): "let $(a_t)$ be a bounded **deterministic** sequence", summands stationary and centred. Confirmed verbatim.

2) All three SA applications use random, data-dependent, F_{t-1}-measurable weights:
 - thm:as (l.128-133): "$a_t=\gamma_t\opnorm{P_{t-1}}\norm{\nabla F(\theta_{t-1})}$" — random. Worse, the scalar being summed is $\nabla F(\theta_{t-1})^\top P_{t-1}\eps_t$, i.e. a random *direction* applied to $\eps_t$, which is not of the form $a_t\zeta_t$ at all even for deterministic $a_t$. The excuse "a localisation argument ... removes the dependence of the weights on the future" only buys boundedness/adaptedness, not determinism.

VERIFIED PREMISE. I fetched https://arxiv.org/abs/2604.10814. The abstract confirms the finding's factual claim: "a trajectory-regression estimator--which estimates the Hessian by regressing SGD increments on iterates--achieves O(n^{-(1-alpha)/2}), matching the lower bound." So Ni & Huo's own minimax-optimal estimator does form a Hessian estimate, and "Hessian-free" there means no direct second-derivative oracle / measurable w.r.t. the SGD trajectory. Forming or maintaining a curvature estimate therefore does not by itself put an estimator outside the class.

- /Volumes/Crucial X6/MacBook/Code/ml_papers/streaming_qn_dependent/paper/main.tex l.197-200: "This does not contradict the minimax rate for Hessian-free covariance estimation from an SGD trajectory \citep{ni2026online}: a quasi-Newton method is not in that class, because it already maintains curvature and forms block gradients." -- the only genuinely loose clause. "it already maintains curvature" is not a distinguishing property; "and forms block gradients" is.

WHY NOT MAJOR. (1) The escape itself is valid and trivially defensible: main.tex l.286-290 builds curvature from the exact per-sample Hessian terms alpha_i Phi_i Phi_i^T (with nabla^2 F = E[alpha Phi Phi^T], l.123, l.361), i.e. BGSN literally has direct Hessian access plus per-observation gradients -- exactly the information the Hessian-free/trajectory-only class forbids. (2) No theorem, rate, or claim depends on the clause -- it is a non-contradiction disclaimer, and the paper explicitly renounces optimality within its own information set. The code asymmetry is real and I demonstrated it directly: in src/bgsn/_core.py the plug-in accumulator (244-250) runs in pass 1 of every block and increments n_plugin unconditionally, before the `if warm: ... continue` (259-273) that skips the S_bm/S_ft accrual. Running streaming_newton with n_warm=T-1 returns Gamma0_hat exactly equal to N^-1 sum y_i^2 x_i x_i' (max diff 5e-15), proving warm-up observations are scored at the frozen theta_0=0 and are averaged in. Measured on AR-hom (d=20, N=200k, b=20, n_warm=50 -> 1000 obs = 0.50%), 6 seeds, using the exact decomposition S_post = N*G0_impl - sum_{i<n_warm*b} y^2 x x': mean diag(H^-1 G0 H^-1)/truth = 1.0175 +/- 0.0026 as implemented (matches the finding) versus 1.0047 +/- 0.0027 with warm-up dropped (the finding's 0.9940 is wrong). So the effect is +1.28% variance / +0.64% SE / +0.0030 in plug-in coverage, not +2.35%/+0.9%/+0.004 — about 1.8x overstated. Severity should drop to minor: (a) exp2's own Monte Carlo SE is ~0.009 (per-replicate coverage sd ~0.152 at R=300), so the systematic offset is ~1/3 of one MC SE and moves the sweep max from ~0.017 to ~0.019, inside the noise; (b) the bias raises the dependence-blind competitor's coverage, so it understates the failure the paper documents rather than flattering the paper's method; (c) no theoretical claim is affected — n_warm*b = warm_mult*d = 1000 observations is fixed in N (estimators.py:133), so the contamination is O(d/N) and Gamma0hat ->p Gamma0 still holds, which is all prop:coverage needs; (d) nothing is mis-quoted: paper/numbers.tex:11 still has \providecommand{\CovLawMaxErr}{[TBD]} and results/exp2_coverage_law.json does not exist (the .log is empty), so exp2 has not been run and the finding's "re-quote" framing is inaccurate. The claimed real-data amplification does not hold either: metro protocol A has 15% warm-up but the implemented plug-in SE comes out *below* the warm-dropped one (ratio 0.92) in 4 of 6 segments, and within-segment orc.H is numerically singular there. Still worth the one-line guard (`if want_plugin == 1 and not warm:`) before the final exp2/exp1 runs so Gamma0_hat and S_ft see the same observations.
